newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus plays down talk of military accord.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus plays down talk of military accord.

text.p: Cyprus on Tuesday dismissed as a "misunderstanding" U.S. talk of an imminent breakthrough in a military dialogue to reduce tension along the ceasefire line dividing Greek and Turkish Cypriots.

"There has not been any agreement other than that which was already in place, that the military dialogue would continue based on what is stipulated in the relevant resolution of the United Nations," Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides told reporters.
U.S. envoy Carey Cavanaugh and State Department spokesman Nicolas Burns said in Cyprus and Washington respectively on Monday that an agreement was close.
But hours later, Cypriot officials said the "agreement" was in fact a promise of political support for the dialogue, which has been going on under U.N. auspices for several months.
"There must have been a misunderstanding in Mr Burns's briefing," said Yiannakis Cassoulides, the Cypriot government spokesman.

"President Clerides has reiterated to Mr Cavanaugh his intention to intervene in the military dialogue with our own military people and see what is happening with the dialogue and try to help it to advance. That's all," he said.
Cavanaugh was sent to the island to defuse a row over Cyprus's decision to buy Russian anti-aircraft missiles and Turkish threats of a military strike to stop their deployment.

The U.N. proposals relate to the unloading of live ammunition among troops on either side of the 180-km (110-mile) ceasefire line and unmanning sentry posts. They also impose a code of conduct for soldiers to follow.
Four Greek Cypriots and one Turkish Cypriot soldier have been killed in incidents along the U.N.-patrolled buffer zone since June, greatly raising tension between the two sides.
U.N. spokesman Waldemar Rokoszewski said the intentions of the two sides on dialogue would be more apparent in separate meetings at the end of the week with officials from either side.
"During discussions so far, both sides indicated their priorities, which are not always compatible," he said.

The United States is trying to broker another agreement aimed at stopping Greek and Turkish military overflights. Greek planes occasionally train in Cypriot airspace within the framework of a 1993 defence agreement between the two countries.
Cassoulides said Cyprus's agreement would depend on Turkey's commitment to suspend its own military flights without reserving the right to resume them.

The U.S. envoy said the military dialogue proposals would help ease tension. "Both sides today gave their support to very quick and immediate implementation of that pack of proposals," Cavanaugh said on Monday evening before leaving for Athens for more talks on Cyprus.
Turkey had threatened military action several times last week to stop deployment of the S-300 missile system, which the Cypriot government says is purely defensive.

Cavanaugh earlier said the crisis in Cyprus had been defused because its government had assured him it would not bring in any part of the missile system for at least 16 months, a fact that the U.S. State Department was aware of before his visit.
Washington strongly criticised Cyprus last week for the deal, but said any Turkish response would be unacceptable.
"My guess is that the Americans came along and created the crisis to come back later and say they defused it," said one diplomat.

Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded the north of the island after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece. Turkey has about 30,000 troops in the north while the internationally recognised Cypriot government has 11,500 in the south.
